newsitem.title: USA: U.S. will not fuel "war fever" in Saudi blast.
newsitem.headline: U.S. will not fuel "war fever" in Saudi blast.

text.p: The United States said on Thursday it was still investigating a deadly truck bomb attack in Saudi Arabia and declined "to fuel any war fever" over speculation about U.S. retaliation against Iran if it is found to be involved.

"I don't want to fuel any war fever that seems to be growing in the press right now," Pentagon spokesman Ken Bacon said when asked about a Los Angeles Times report that contingency plans were under way for possible retaliation, including military strikes, against Iran.

The June 20 blast that killed 19 U.S. troops at Khobar Towers housing complex in Dhahran is still under investigation and President Bill Clinton is not in a position to consider any counter-measures, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

Asked if the Pentagon had contingency plans for a military move against Iran, McCurry told reporters there were plans for "any possible, imaginable contingency" because "that's what military planners do."
"I wouldn't read too much into it," he added.
The Los Angeles Times on Thursday said U.S. law enforcement and Pentagon officials had tentatively concluded that Saudi Shiites were responsible for the bombing.

The newspaper said possible U.S. punitive actions against Iran included retaliatory strikes on military targets but it stressed that Washington lacked sufficient proof to support Saudi Arabia's contention that Shiites trained and armed by Iran carried out the attack.

In Jakarta on Thursday, Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati denied Iran was involved in bomb attacks and said U.S. efforts to isolate his country had failed. "It is a baseless allegation," he said of U.S. media reports linking Iran to two bomb attacks on U.S. military installations in Saudi Arabia in which a total of 24 Americans were killed.
Velayati said Iran believed the bombings in Saudi Arabia were an internal problem of the kingdom.

In Washington, Bacon was asked about previous comments by Secretary of Defence William Perry that appropriate action would be taken by the United States if another country or countries were found to be behind the bombing.
"The president has spoken about the response we will take and the secretary has spoken about the response we will take. Nothing has changed about that," Bacon said.

U.S. defence officials, who asked not to be identified, also declined comment on a Washington Post report this week that the Saudis had told FBI Director Louis Freeh they were convinced the attack was carried out by Saudi extremists with support from Iran.
"We don't discuss such matters, and we certainly aren't about to discuss anything about an FBI investigation that isn't over yet," one of the officials said.
Deputy Defence Secretary John White told reporters in response to questions on Thursday that Freeh had not completed his investigation and had not submitted a report to Clinton.

"Mr. Freeh is involved and I have talked to him as recently as last week in the continuing investigation with respect to Khobar Towers," White said. "He (Freeh) certainly has not completed that review and therefore he has not made his report to the president. And we don't know what those results will be or exactly when they will come out."
